"'''Arkangel'''" is the second episode of the fourth series of the British science fiction [[anthology series]] ''[[Black Mirror]]''. Written by series creator and showrunner [[Charlie Brooker]] and directed by [[Jodie Foster]], it premiered on [[Netflix]] on 29 December 2017, along with the rest of series four. In the episode, the single mother Marie ([[Rosemarie DeWitt]]) enrolls her daughter Sara in a trial of Arkangel, an implanted technology which allows Marie to track Sara's location, current vision and hearing, and automatically censors distressing material.

The main theme of the episode is [[helicopter parenting]]; as a woman raised by a single mother, Foster had many views which influenced the script, such as a more complex characterisation of Marie, and was given control of casting. For the filming in November 2016, Foster chose a location in Canada to represent working-class America. Differently aged versions of Sara are played by different actors, with [[Brenna Harding]] playing her as a teenager.

Critics saw Marie as a parent afflicted with much anxiety and guilt and compared Arkangel to existing technologies for child monitoring, such as [[microchip implant (human)|microchip implants]] and [[smartwatches]]. They were mostly laudatory of Foster's directing style and DeWitt's acting but less complimentary of the storyline and moral, which were seen as simplistic, with many reviewers suggesting themes the episode could have explored in more detail. In one scene, a nurse incorrectly implies that an [[emergency contraception]] (EC) pill induces abortion, rather than preventing pregnancy. The episode was poorly received in comparison to other ''Black Mirror'' episodes.

==Plot==
Single mother Marie Sambrell ([[Rosemarie DeWitt]]) gives birth to her daughter Sara and raises her with help from Sara's grandfather, Russ ([[Nicholas Campbell]]). Three-year-old Sara (Aniya Hodge) gets lost following a cat and a distressed Marie has to enlist help from neighbours to locate her. Afterwards, Marie signs her up for a trial of Arkangel, a child monitoring system installed via an implant. Marie can monitor Sara's vision and hearing with a [[tablet computer]], along with viewing live medical data and past audiovisual feeds. A filter can censor stimuli when they cause Sara stress, such as an intimidating neighbourhood dog. Shortly after, Russ survives a [[stroke]], because Marie is notified when Sara, observing Russ, experiences stress.

Six years later, Russ has died. A classmate named Ryan "Trick" Tribecky (Nicky Torchia) tries to show Sara (Sarah Abbott) sexual and violent imagery but the filter blurs it. Sara draws blood from her finger, trying to learn what it looks like, so Marie has her assessed by a psychologist who recommends that she dispose of Arkangel, which is soon to be banned. Marie deactivates the filter and stores the tablet in the attic. An anxious Sara goes to school unsupervised and Trick shows her pornography and gore videos.

Aged fifteen, Sara ([[Brenna Harding]]) lies to her mother about going to a friend's house to attend a party with Trick ([[Owen Teague]]). Marie discovers the lie and after failing to contact her, turns on Arkangel. She sees Sara having sex for the first time, with Trick. Marie starts to use the tablet again and soon sees Sara snorting [[cocaine]] that Trick—who deals drugs—gives her.

Identifying Trick with a [[reverse image search]], Marie confronts him at work and blackmails him to stay away from Sara. After receiving an Arkangel notification that Sara is pregnant, Marie sneaks an [[emergency contraceptive]] pill into Sara's smoothie. She later vomits and is told by a nurse that the pill caused it. Sara confronts Marie and forces the tablet away from her. The stress filter is accidentally reactivated. Unable to see the damage she is causing, Sara beats Marie unconscious with the tablet, breaking it.

The filter deactivates and Sara runs away. When Marie regains consciousness, she frantically yells for Sara down the street. A hitch-hiking Sara gets into a truck.

==Production==
Whilst series one and two of ''Black Mirror'' were shown on [[Channel 4]] in the UK, in September 2015 Netflix commissioned the series for 12 episodes,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2015/digital/news/netflix-black-mirror-new-episodes-1201602037/|title='Black Mirror' Lands at Netflix|first=Debra|last=Birnbaum|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=25 September 2015|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612162641/https://variety.com/2015/digital/news/netflix-black-mirror-new-episodes-1201602037/|url-status=live}}</ref> and in March 2016 it outbid Channel 4 for the rights to distribute the series in the UK, with a bid of $40&nbsp;million.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2016/mar/29/netflix-channel-4-charlie-brooker-black-mirror |title=Netflix deals Channel 4 knockout blow over Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror |first=John |last=Plunkett |date=29 March 2016 |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=12 January 2021 |archive-date=30 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171230021155/https://www.theguardian.com/media/2016/mar/29/netflix-channel-4-charlie-brooker-black-mirror |url-status=live }}</ref> The 12-episode order was divided into two series of six episodes each, with "Arkangel" in the latter group. The six episodes in series four were released on Netflix simultaneously on 29 December 2017.<ref name="RT interview">{{cite web|url=http://www.radiotimes.com/news/on-demand/2017-12-07/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-episode-guide/|title=Black Mirror season 4 episode guide: Charlie Brooker reveals new plot and episode details|website=[[Radio Times]]|last=Ling|first=Thomas|date=7 December 2017|access-date=2 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171210155309/http://www.radiotimes.com/news/on-demand/2017-12-07/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-episode-guide/|archive-date=10 December 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> "Arkangel" is listed as the second episode, but as ''Black Mirror'' is an [[anthology series]], each instalment can be watched in any order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bustle.com/p/watch-the-black-mirror-season-4-episodes-in-this-order-for-the-best-viewing-experience-7690945|title=Watch The 'Black Mirror' Season 4 Episodes In This Order For The Best Viewing Experience|website=[[Bustle (magazine)|Bustle]]|last=Thomas|first=Leah|date=29 December 2017|access-date=2 September 2018|archive-date=2 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902143829/https://www.bustle.com/p/watch-the-black-mirror-season-4-episodes-in-this-order-for-the-best-viewing-experience-7690945|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Writing===
The episode was written by series creator [[Charlie Brooker]]. Executive producer [[Annabel Jones]] said that it was inspired by [[microchip implant (animal)|microchip implants]] used to identify pets that, at the time of writing, were also being considered for children. Jones said, "We wanted to think what the updated version of that [was] and find a really good idea of how that could go terribly wrong".<ref>{{Cite web | url = https://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-annabel-jones-interview-1202644294/ | title = 'Black Mirror' Co-Creator Breaks Down Season 4: 'We Want to Be Surprising and Unpredictable' | first = Danielle | last = Turchiano | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 1 January 2018 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] | archive-date = 31 December 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171231233828/http://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-annabel-jones-interview-1202644294/ | url-status = live }}</ref> The episode is intended to be sympathetic to [[helicopter parenting]]; Brooker took inspiration in how protective he felt following the birth of his children.<ref name="ew interview"/><ref name="vice brooker"/> Prior to having children, Brooker thought negatively of content restrictions designed for children, but he was concerned by his three-year-old son seeing a horror movie trailer after he left him alone with [[YouTube]] on autoplay. He was also concerned by thoughts of his children seeing an accident or hearing profanity in their day-to-day life.<ref name="ibm">{{cite book | title=  Inside Black Mirror | date = November 2018 | first1 = Charlie | last1 = Brooker | first2 = Annabel | last2 = Jones | first3 = Jason | last3 = Arnopp | chapter = Arkangel | isbn = 9781984823489 | publisher =  [[Crown Publishing Group]] | place = New York City }}</ref>

===Director and casting===
[[File:Jodie Foster Césars 2011 2 (cropped).jpg|right|thumb|upright|alt=Jodie Foster|"Arkangel" was directed by [[Jodie Foster]], making it the first episode of ''Black Mirror'' to be directed by a woman.]]
The actor, director and producer [[Jodie Foster]] directed ''Black Mirror''; previous credits included episodes of the Netflix series ''[[Orange Is the New Black]]'' and ''[[House of Cards (American TV series)|House of Cards]]''.<ref name="vice brooker">{{cite web | url = https://www.vice.com/en/article/charlie-brooker-discusses-the-arkangel-episode-of-black-mirror/ | title = Charlie Brooker Discusses the 'Arkangel' Episode of 'Black Mirror' | first = Sam | last = Wolfson | date = 10 January 2018 | access-date = 10 January 2018 | work = [[Vice (magazine)|Vice]] }}</ref> Foster was introduced to ''Black Mirror'' by Netflix's vice president of original content after telling her that she enjoyed directing short but complete stories, in contrast to serialised television programmes.<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Brooker saw Foster as suited to "Arkangel" because as a former [[child actor]], she would understand what it was like to grow up in the spotlight.<ref name="vice brooker"/><ref name="RTepisodeguide">{{cite web|url=http://www.radiotimes.com/news/on-demand/2017-12-07/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-episode-guide/|title=Black Mirror season 4 episode guide: Charlie Brooker reveals new plot and episode details|work=[[Radio Times]]|last=Ling|first=Thomas|date=7 December 2017|access-date=10 December 2017|archive-date=10 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171210155309/http://www.radiotimes.com/news/on-demand/2017-12-07/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-episode-guide/|url-status=live}}</ref> Foster was raised by a single mother, and said that the script brought up "so many questions about who we are as women at this particular time in history".<ref name="ibm"/> She was the first woman to direct a ''Black Mirror'' episode.<ref name="indiewire">{{cite web|url=http://www.indiewire.com/2017/12/black-mirror-jodie-foster-arkangel-interview-rosemary-dewitt-1201911258/|title='Black Mirror': Jodie Foster on Directing Season 4's 'Arkangel' Like 'A Really Small Indie Movie'|work=[[IndieWire]]|last=Miller|first=Liz Shannon|date=28 December 2017|access-date=28 December 2017}}</ref>

Foster was in control of casting the episode and also hiring much of the production crew.<ref name="BuzzFeed">{{cite web|url=https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/kateaurthur/black-mirror-arkangel-jodie-foster-season-4|title=Everything You Need To Know About The "Black Mirror" Episode "Arkangel"|work=[[BuzzFeed News]]|last=Aurthur|first=Kate|date=29 December 2017|access-date=2 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222354/https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/kateaurthur/black-mirror-arkangel-jodie-foster-season-4|url-status=live}}</ref> She cast her friend Rosemarie DeWitt as Marie. The pair had met through Foster's wife [[Alexandra Hedison]]; this was only the second time Foster had directed a friend, after [[Mel Gibson]] in the 2011 film ''[[The Beaver (film)|The Beaver]]''.<ref name="indiewire"/> The Australian actor Brenna Harding was cast as Sara, after misinterpreting part of the audition tape instructions and performing a two-minute monologue in the character of Sara, rather than as herself. The three other children cast as younger versions of Sara had to be chosen to look very similar to Harding.<ref name="ibm"/> Foster was experienced in directing child actors and said that much of the skill lay in casting.<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Owen Teague's role as Trick influenced the character: though written as a character to be distrusted, Foster said that Teague has "sweetness" and Harding described Trick and Sara as "like two old souls who connected".<ref name="ibm"/>

The original script gave Marie's father only a very minor part, but this was fleshed out by Foster. She also influenced other changes in the script, and offered many observations on the technology used and Marie's motivation for her actions after seeing her daughter have sex with Trick.<ref name="ew interview">{{cite magazine|url=http://ew.com/tv/2017/12/29/black-mirror-jodie-foster-arkangel/|title=''Black Mirror'' creator reveals what Jodie Foster changed in 'Arkangel'|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Hibberd|first=James|date=29 December 2017|access-date=31 December 2017|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222353/https://ew.com/tv/2017/12/29/black-mirror-jodie-foster-arkangel/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="ibm"/> In contrast to Jones and Brooker's more positive conception of Marie, Foster was informed by her life experience to show a darkness to her character.<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Explaining the actions of her character Marie, DeWitt said that single mothers "experience betrayal differently". Foster added that when Marie realises Sara is lying to her but does not confront her, it causes a "fissure" and Marie begins "fighting a battle to win control". By attempting to prevent her daughter from leaving her, Marie is victim to a [[self-fulfilling prophecy]] as she "engendered the exact result that she most feared".<ref name="variety interview">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-jodie-foster-rosemarie-dewitt-interview-1202596197/|title='Black Mirror': Jodie Foster and Rosemarie DeWitt on the 'Dark' Mother/Daughter Dynamic of 'Arkangel'|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Turchiano|first=Danielle|date=29 December 2017|access-date=30 December 2017|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222235/https://variety.com/2017/tv/news/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-jodie-foster-rosemarie-dewitt-interview-1202596197/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Filming and editing===
{{multiple image|total_width=300
| image1 = Rosemarie DeWitt.jpg
| alt1   = Rosemarie DeWitt
| image2 = Brenna Harding (8367451094).jpg
| alt2   = Brenna Harding
| footer = [[Rosemarie DeWitt]] ''(left)'' starred as Marie while [[Brenna Harding]] ''(right)'' starred as her daughter Sara during her teenage years.
}}
The episode was filmed across three weeks in November 2016.<ref name="hwr interview"/> A location in [[Hamilton, Ontario]], was chosen by Foster to depict blue-collar America.<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Jones was present for filming but Brooker was not.<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Foster described the fictional setting as a "place that used to have a foundation and a glory", which reflects how Marie views herself.<ref name="ibm"/> She stated that the filming involved "very long hours" and that the scenes starring the younger children were particularly troublesome.<ref name="indiewire"/> Graphic content was mostly avoided in the episode, with Foster believing it would "distract from what the meaning was". An exception was the scene where Sara attacks her mother.<ref name="variety interview"/> Brooker noted that in this scene, more hits were filmed than made it into the episode, though enough were needed in the final cut for the viewer to understand Sara's perspective, and for Marie to be plausibly rendered unconscious.<ref name="ew interview"/> The final shot of the episode, where Marie frantically tries to use the tablet shouting "No!" repeatedly, was filmed the day after the [[2016 United States presidential election|presidential election]] results were known and [[Donald Trump]] became president-elect; DeWitt injected her personal reaction at the results into the scene.<ref name="hwr interview">{{Cite web | url = https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/black-mirror-season-4-director-jodie-foster-arkangel-episode-1070594 | title = 'Black Mirror': How Jodie Foster and Rosemarie DeWitt Made Their Story Personal | first = Jackie | last =Strauss | date = 29 December 2017 | access-date = 4 January 2018 | work = [[The Hollywood Reporter]] }}</ref>

Foster described the ending as a "parable".<ref name="ibm"/> DeWitt's first day on set was to film the scene where a bloodied Marie runs out of the house screaming for her daughter. The episode ends with Sara entering a truck, which was originally a small car in the script. The choice of a truck implies that Sara will be travelling far, and Harding felt "a mixture of nervous trepidation and excitement for Sara".<ref name="ibm"/> Foster said: "I want her to close that door on this chapter, this town, on that relationship, and become who she is."<ref name="BuzzFeed"/> Foster flew to London to help Brooker with the episode's editing—the first time she had met him.<ref name="vice brooker"/><ref name="BuzzFeed"/> The song "[[I'm a Mother]]" by [[the Pretenders]] plays during the credits, chosen as a "plaintive song" which reminds viewers of "the mother's perspective", according to Foster.<ref name="ibm"/>

==Analysis==
As intended by Foster, critics saw the episode as being set in working-class America.<ref name="ibm"/> ''[[The Atlantic]]''{{'}}s [[Sophie Gilbert]] found it "set in a nondescript EveryTown USA" and "deliberately muted".<ref name="Atlantic">{{cite web|title=''Black Mirror'': 'Arkangel' Mines the Horror of Helicopter Parenting|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2017/12/black-mirror-arkangel-mines-the-horror-of-helicopter-parenting/549368/|work=[[The Atlantic]]|last=Gilbert|first=Sophie|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|url-access=limited|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222242/https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2017/12/black-mirror-arkangel-mines-the-horror-of-helicopter-parenting/549368/|url-status=live}}</ref> Steve O'Brien of ''[[Digital Spy]]'' saw it as more "thrillingly, authentically American" than any prior episode.<ref name="DS">{{cite web|url=https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/ustv/a845720/black-mirror-arkangel-review-season-4/|title=Black Mirror season 4 'ArkAngel' review: A cautionary tale that feels more like an indie movie|work=[[Digital Spy]]|last=O'Brien|first=Steve|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref> Louisa Mellor of ''[[Den of Geek]]'' found that the blue-collar setting contrasts with most previous episodes' depictions of "shiny near-futures, in chic, modernist homes". She also highlighted the episode as the most female-heavy with regard to characters to that point.<ref name="DoG">{{cite web|url=https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-review/|title=Black Mirror season 4: Arkangel review|work=[[Den of Geek]]|last=Mellor|first=Louisa|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222239/https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-review/|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]''{{'}}s Jacob Oller commented that the camera shows multiple perspectives throughout the episode: first-person, third-person and first-person from another person's perspective. Oller saw this as giving the episode a [[horror film|horror]] feel, heightened by the "long-short-long editing" pattern of "tension, release, rebuild".<ref name="Paste">{{cite web|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-review-arkangel/|title=''Black Mirror'' Review: Rosemarie DeWitt Shines in the Jodie Foster-Directed "Arkangel"|work=[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]|last=Oller|first=Jacob|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222257/https://www.pastemagazine.com/tv/black-mirror/black-mirror-review-arkangel/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Caroline Framke]] of ''[[Vox (website)|Vox]]'' saw Foster's directing as "generally stark and matter-of-fact", though a handheld camera is used when characters are in "a particular state of panic" so that the framing shows "their confused and rapidly fracturing relationship to each other and the world around them".<ref name="Vox">{{cite web|url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2017/12/29/16791518/black-mirror-arkangel-recap-season-4-review|title=Black Mirror's "Arkangel" takes parental surveillance to its darkest, most obvious 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222300/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-episode-2-spoiler-review-netflix-tablet-tracker-a8131386.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

The episode has a theme of [[helicopter parent]]ing. ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''{{'}}s Darren Franich saw it as a "straightforward parable"; both Franich and ''[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]''{{'}}s Charles Bramesco compared the episode to an [[after school special]] due to its simple moral message.<ref name="EW">{{cite magazine|url=https://ew.com/tv/2017/12/06/black-mirror-review/|title=''Black Mirror'' season 4: EW reviews all six episodes|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|last=Franich|first=Darren|date=6 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=25 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200325203100/https://ew.com/tv/2017/12/06/black-mirror-review/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Vulture">{{cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2017/12/black-mirror-season-4-recap-arkangel.html|title=''Black Mirror'' Recap: Parents Just Don't Understand|work=[[Vulture (magazine)|Vulture]]|last=Bramesco|first=Charles|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222252/https://www.vulture.com/2017/12/black-mirror-season-4-recap-arkangel.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', Sonia Saraiya wrote that it was "so blatant it could bludgeon you", the message being: "If you love it, let it go".<ref name="Variety">{{cite web|url=https://variety.com/2017/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-tv-review-1202648385/|title=TV Review: 'Black Mirror' Season 4 on Netflix|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|last=Saraiya|first=Sonia|date=23 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=3 February 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200203154600/https://variety.com/2017/tv/reviews/black-mirror-season-4-netflix-tv-review-1202648385/|url-status=live}}</ref> Mellor found that relevant questions raised include where the "right to privacy and agency" of a child overrides the "power of a parent", and whether pain is an "instructive" or "traumatising" formative experience.<ref name="DoG"/> Framke saw the episode as a case of the programme's "overall ethos that pretty much everything we try in the name of protecting ourselves and each other will eventually, inevitably backfire", in that Marie trying to shield Sara is only "a temporary salve".<ref name="Vox"/> Bramesco compared the episode's storyline to that of ''[[Spring Awakening (play)|Spring Awakening]]'', a 1906 play later adapted into [[Spring Awakening (musical)|a 2000s musical]]: the play depicts teenagers developing sexual awareness after a lack of parental sex education.<ref name="Vulture"/> Gilbert commented on a similarity between the Arkangel's functionality and that of the Z-Eyes from the ''Black Mirror'' episode "[[White Christmas (Black Mirror)|White Christmas]]".<ref name="Atlantic"/>

[[File:Child's phone watch (smartwatch) in China (boy).jpg|upright=1.25|alt=Child wearing a smartwatch|thumb|''[[The Guardian]]''{{'}}s Zoe Williams compared Arkangel to existing [[smartwatches]] designed for children.<ref name="Guardian"/>]]

Critics identified various technologies in the real world as relevant to the episode's themes. Oller compared Arkangel to [[radio-frequency identification]] (RFID) implants used in animals, while Tasha Robinson of ''[[The Verge]]'' commented that such implants have been [[Microchip implant (human)|used in humans]].<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="Verge">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/8/16864378/black-mirror-arkangel-season-4-jodie-foster-rosemarie-dewitt-review-analysis|title=Black Mirror's Arkangel misses out on so many story opportunities|work=[[The Verge]]|last=Robinson|first=Tasha|date=8 January 2018|access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref> Robinson further noted that there have been "a long-running series of debates" over the morality of using the implants in children.<ref name="Verge"/> Zoe Williams commented in ''[[The Guardian]]'' that [[GPS]] monitoring for children is frequently marketed in the form of a [[smartwatch]], some of which can listen into the wearer's conversations. She found the underlying principle behind the technology to be "that your perception of your child's vulnerability takes precedence over their interaction with the world".<ref name="Guardian">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2018/jan/03/black-mirror-shows-whos-really-losing-their-minds-in-the-digital-age-parents|title=Black Mirror shows who's really losing their minds in the digital age – parents|last=Williams|first=Zoe|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=3 January 2018|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222255/https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2018/jan/03/black-mirror-shows-whos-really-losing-their-minds-in-the-digital-age-parents|url-status=live}}</ref> Robinson noted that clothing with trackers and third-party monitoring and control of a mobile phone are other technologies targeted at parents.<ref name="Verge"/>

The opening scene in which Marie gives birth serves to show her anxieties as a parent. Gilbert said that she feels "frantic" and briefly thinks her baby has died, which is "every parent's worst fear".<ref name="Atlantic"/> Mellor said that it shows Marie "feels anxiety and guilt over not being a good-enough mother" even before she begins parenting.<ref name="DoG"/> Robinson analysed that the episode uses the scene "as a frame for how [Marie] projects her fears of inadequacy onto her daughter".<ref name="Verge"/> O'Brien saw the doctor's line "cutting the umbilical cord" as reflecting symbolism that for Marie, "it never was cut".<ref name="DS"/> Mellor said that Marie's isolation as a single parent, ill father and long working hours are all contributing factors to her guilt.<ref name="DoG"/> Similarly, O'Brien commented that Marie has little in her life outside of Sara and that few of her interactions with Sara "aren't finger-wagging".<ref name="DS"/> Bramesco saw Marie as "the one at fault" in the episode, with Trick portrayed as "a pretty decent guy" and Sara's drug usage not being seen as "scandalizing".<ref name="Vulture"/>

The reproductive healthcare organisation [[Planned Parenthood]] criticised the depiction of emergency contraceptive (EC) pills as inaccurate. A nurse tells Sara that the purpose of such a pill is "terminating your pregnancy", but this is a description of [[abortion]] rather than [[contraception]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.newsweek.com/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-abortion-morning-after-pill-771307|title=Planned Parenthood Responds to Jodie Foster's Inaccurate 'Black Mirror' Abortion Episode|work=[[Newsweek]]|last=Gaudette|first=Emily|date=4 January 2018|access-date=7 January 2018|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222256/https://www.newsweek.com/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-abortion-morning-after-pill-771307|url-status=live}}</ref> Contraception prevents the fertilisation of an egg before a person becomes pregnant.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://screenrant.com/black-mirror-jodie-foster-arkangel-controversy/|title=Black Mirror: Why Jodie Foster's "Arkangel" Was So Controversial|work=[[Screen Rant]]|last=Phillips|first=Marian|date=2 June 2020|access-date=2 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222312/https://screenrant.com/black-mirror-jodie-foster-arkangel-controversy/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
The episode received mixed reception. The review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]] gives the episode a 78% rating based on 23 critics, with the summary: "Though a bit too on the nose, 'Arkangel' brings balance to ''Black Mirror''{{'}}s typically frenetic episodes with a calm, contemplative, and compelling installment."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e02|title=Black Mirror – Season 4, Episode 1 – Rotten Tomatoes|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=12 January 2021|archive-date=12 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210112222300/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/black_mirror/s04/e02|url-status=live}}</ref> ''[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]'' awarded it three out of five stars while ''Vulture'' gave it two.<ref name="Vulture"/><ref name="Telegraph"/> ''Paste'' rated it 8.6 out of 10 and ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' gave it a B+.<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="AVClub"/> Robinson found it the "weakest" episode of the fourth series.<ref name="Verge"/>

Critics were split on the episode's storyline and message. Gilbert saw the premise as "potent" and Mellor as "solid", but Robinson saw the story as "simplistic".<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="DoG"/><ref name="Verge"/> Bramesco saw it as "too far-fetched to accept" that the Arkangel technology could be developed and used despite "such glaring potential for calamity and/or human-rights violations".<ref name="Vulture"/> Saraiya found the story "well-done" and O'Brien found the ending "beautifully ambiguous".<ref name="DS"/><ref name="Variety"/> ''The A.V. Club''{{'}}s Zach Handlen viewed the narrative arc as unsurprising but said that "the specifics make it compelling"; he reviewed that the moral is "hard to argue with" but "not really unexpected".<ref name="AVClub">{{cite web|url=https://www.avclub.com/black-mirror-explores-the-downside-of-parental-controls-1821634112|title=Black Mirror explores the downside of parental controls|work=[[The A.V. Club]]|last=Handlen|first=Zach|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021}}</ref> Gilbert found the moral "increasingly obvious" once Sara lies to her mother about where she is going out for the evening, whilst Robinson said that the episode's "sheer earnestness makes its simplicity and obviousness even more awkward".<ref name="Atlantic"/><ref name="Verge"/> Handlen saw the conclusion as obvious in the context of past ''Black Mirror'' episodes, which "robs the episode of freshness or surprise".<ref name="AVClub"/>

Many reviewers had criticisms of the episode's execution or focus, with Gilbert finding that the execution is where it "sputters and dies".<ref name="Atlantic"/> Robinson wrote that Brooker "starts a story with infinite potential, then cuts it short just as it’s spinning up".<ref name="Verge"/> Gilbert found the topic of young children being exposed to sexual and violent material from a young age more timely than helicopter parenting.<ref name="Atlantic"/> Ed Power, writing for ''The Telegraph'', similarly found it a "pity Brooker doesn't delve further" into pornography's effects on Sara.<ref name="Telegraph">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/on-demand/0/black-mirror-season-4-arkangel-review-bleak-parental-nightmare/|title=Black Mirror, season 4, Arkangel, review: this bleak parental nightmare needs to grow up|work=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]|last=Power|first=Ed|date=29 December 2017|access-date=12 January 2021|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Robinson also thought it would have been interesting to explore Marie "living through" Sara when she begins young adulthood.<ref name="Verge"/> However, Bramesco praised that the episode is a "rare meditation on the millennial generation that rightly looks to the parents for answers instead of blaming the youth".<ref name="Vulture"/> Hooton saw the film ''[[Men, Women & Children (film)|Men, Women & Children]]'' (2014) as exploring similar themes to "Arkangel" but with stronger execution.<ref name="Independent"/>

Foster's directing and casting was the subject of much commentary. Gilbert wrote that the "lo-fi, indie feel Foster gives the episode captures the terrible ordinariness of the situation", praising "unforgettable images" and "foreboding framing".<ref name="Atlantic"/>
Mellor found that Foster constructed a "sensitive and emotional US indie-movie style", while Handlen noted that she "captures the show's clinical, mournful feel, but manages a necessary level of intimacy that keeps the story from being overly schematic".<ref name="DoG"/><ref name="AVClub"/> In contrast, Hooton saw the episode as "visually flat" and Bramesco wrote that Foster engages in "misunderstanding the emotional timbre a scene should have".<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="Independent"/>

Franich and Power praised the performances as "fine" and "compelling", respectively, with both praising Foster for her direction of the younger actors.<ref name="EW"/><ref name="Telegraph"/> However, Hooton saw the actors as "miscast".<ref name="Independent"/> DeWitt's portrayal of Marie received praise for balancing positive and negative traits, by critics Oller, Handlen and Power.<ref name="Paste"/><ref name="Telegraph"/><ref name="AVClub"/> Mellor praised a "deft balance" in that Brooker and Foster "have taken pains not to demonise, but to create a likeable, easy-to-relate-to character" in Marie.<ref name="DoG"/> Oller praised Marie's confrontation of Trick as "epic, expertly realized and emotionally grounded".<ref name="Paste"/> Contrastingly, Bramesco criticised the climax as "abrupt and melodramatic", resulting in "incredulous snorts" rather than "gasps".<ref name="Vulture"/>

''[[IndieWire]]'' authors ranked the 22 ''Black Mirror'' instalments excluding ''Bandersnatch'' by quality, giving "Arkangel" a position of 20th.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Worst to Best|last1=Greene|first1=Steve|last2=Nguyen|first2=Hanh|last3=Miller|first3=Liz Shannon|work=[[IndieWire]]|date=24 November 2017|access-date=1 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171228022045/http://www.indiewire.com/2017/11/best-black-mirror-episodes-worst-netflix-ranked-1201897973/|archive-date=28 December 2017|url-status=live}}</ref> Eric Anthony Glover of ''[[Entertainment Tonight]]'' found the episode to be 12th-best of the 19 episodes from series one to four.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.etonline.com/every-black-mirror-episode-ranked-worst-best-93082|title=Every 'Black Mirror' Episode Ranked, From Worst to Best|website=[[Entertainment Tonight]]|last=Glover|first=Eric Anthony|date=22 December 2017|access-date=1 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180801004027/https://www.etonline.com/every-black-mirror-episode-ranked-worst-best-93082|archive-date=1 August 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref> Instead of by quality, Proma Khosla of ''[[Mashable]]'' ranked the episodes by tone, concluding that "Arkangel" is the 11th-most pessimistic episode of the show.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread|title=Every 'Black Mirror' episode ever, ranked by overall dread|work=[[Mashable]]|last=Khosla|first=Proma|date=5 January 2018|access-date=14 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180308090919/https://mashable.com/2018/01/05/black-mirror-pessimism-ranking-dread/|archive-date=8 March 2018|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Awards===

For his work on "Arkangel", Malcolm McCulloch was nominated for a [[Location Managers Guild Awards]] in the category of Outstanding Locations in a Contemporary Television Series.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/location-managers-guild-awards-nominees-2018-1079654/item/outstanding-locations-a-contemporary-tv-series-1079741 |title='Baby Driver,' 'Dunkirk' Take Location Managers Guild Awards |last=Giardina |first=Carolyn |date=7 April 2018 |website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |access-date=9 April 2018 |archive-date=28 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628233504/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lists/location-managers-guild-awards-nominees-2018-1079654/item/outstanding-locations-a-contemporary-tv-series-1079741 |url-status=live }}</ref>
